personas.why: The flickering knee dot lets me see the bug before the fix is explained. I'd save the diagram for the part where the system decides not to guess.
Fourteen versus eleven gives me a discrepancy I can check for myself. Once the count reconciles, the textbook card feels like the start of another reel.
I stay to see what went wrong with the lift. Once I've seen the circled joint, I'm not curious enough about how the dots were made.
The moving skeleton buys a few more seconds. When the graph starts counting reps, I still want to know what I should actually notice in a workout.
The knee bend turning into a wave is lovely: I understand the graph without having to read it. The corrected count feels like a natural ending.
Watching a bad prediction turn into a fix I can understand makes this feel like a project I could try. I'd send it to my project partner.
I stay to see whether using a personal baseline changes the call. The final freeze gives me essentially the same rep and fault I saw at the start.
Throwing out frames the camera couldn't read earns my attention. But what qualified the green set as 'best'? The verdict depends on that more than on the neat overlay.
I like seeing one messy clip turn into a three-way decision. I'd pause on the process diagram, but 'form-check skill' isn't clear enough to make me comment.
Comparing me with my own best is the interesting choice. I'd rather see a rep where that changes the decision than read a pipeline ending in three coloured labels.
The 14-to-11 strike-through stops my thumb a second time. The last STOP stamp doesn't: I already got that reveal in the opening.
The red correction is a visual I'll remember. By the second title card, though, I've lost track of whether the miscounted set is also the dangerous one.
Showing exactly what blocked the tracker is better than a polished happy-path demo. I'd comment FORM to see how the visibility check feeds the final call.
I'd watch through to see whether 'can't see' survives into the verdict. Matching eleven reps on this clip is a good debugging result, not yet evidence that STOP is reliable.
I watch the actual rep twice. I might send that freeze to another trainer for a second opinion, but a difference from someone's best rep isn't by itself an injury warning.
The red gap over the lifter catches my eye. By the time I'm following a knee graph as well as the face and captions, I've forgotten which set I'm watching.
